html:
The Althing is the general assembly of Iceland, founded in 930 at Thingvellir, a plain in a rift valley east of today's Reykjavík. It is often called the oldest parliament in the world.

The settlers who came from Norway in the settlement of Iceland had no king. Instead the chieftains, called godar, met each summer in the open air for about two weeks. A lawspeaker recited the law from the Law Rock, a third of it each year, a law council made new laws, and courts settled disputes. The meeting was also a fair and a social gathering for the whole island. This system is known as the Icelandic Commonwealth.

In the year 1000 the Althing voted for Iceland to accept Christianity. Feuds among the great families in the 13th century, the age of Snorri Sturluson, ended with Iceland submitting to the king of Norway in 1262 to 1264, after which the Althing became mainly a court. It was abolished in 1800, restored as an advisory body in 1845 in Reykjavík, and won law-making powers again in 1874.
